issue.issue_text: Whether an appellate court, in proceedings for confirmation of a death sentence, must examine the entire record for itself or if it can accept a concession from the defence that there is no substance in the case.

facts: In an appeal against a murder conviction and death sentence, the High Court did not examine the defense evidence.
The High Court's reason for not examining the evidence was that the appellant's own counsel had 'frankly admitted that there was no substance in it'.
The appellant contended before the Supreme Court that the High Court committed an error and failed to properly discharge its duties by not examining the evidence for itself.
law: The Court distinguished between an ordinary criminal appeal and an appeal involving a death sentence confirmation.

In an ordinary appeal (under s. 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure), an appellate court can dismiss the appeal if it finds no sufficient ground for interference, and it is not required to examine the entire record to form its own independent decision.

However, when a High Court hears an appeal from a condemned prisoner, it is also simultaneously dealing with a reference for confirmation of the death sentence under the Code of Criminal Procedure (ss. 374, 375, and 376).
In such cases, the High Court's duty is not merely to see if the lower court's order was correct, but to conduct a complete 're-appraisal and the reassessment of the entire facts and law'.
The High Court must 'examine the case for itself' and 'come to an independent conclusion on the materials' to be satisfied about the guilt or innocence of the accused.
application: The Supreme Court applied the special, heightened standard required for death sentence confirmations to the facts of the case.
It held that the High Court's duty to independently examine the entire record and form its own conclusion cannot be bypassed, even if the defense counsel concedes that their case has no merit.
By accepting the counsel's concession and not examining the defense evidence, the High Court failed to properly discharge its legal duty to conduct a full reappraisal of the case.
The Supreme Court found that there was 'substance in the submission' that the High Court had committed an error.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that in proceedings for the confirmation of a death sentence, an appellate court has a mandatory duty to examine the entire record for itself to arrive at an independent conclusion regarding the guilt of the accused. It cannot abdicate this responsibility by accepting a concession from the defense counsel that there is no substance in the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court can interfere with the sentence awarded by a lower court.

facts: The appellant was convicted of a murder that was not premeditated.
The act was committed by a "hot-headed person" who was incited by his father.
The murder was not considered cruel or brutal.
The Court identified these circumstances as "special features" of the case.
law: Ordinarily, the Supreme Court, exercising its power under Article 136, does not interfere with a sentence handed down by a lower court.
However, the Court may interfere with a sentence in a case that has "special features" where the "ends of justice" would be better met by a different penalty.
application: The Court applied the exception to the general rule, finding that the specific circumstances of the case—the lack of premeditation, the incitement by the appellant's father, and the absence of cruelty—constituted "special features."
Due to these special features, the Court determined that the ends of justice would be met by awarding the lesser penalty of life imprisonment instead of the death sentence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that while it ordinarily does not interfere with sentences, it can and will do so in cases with special features. In this instance, the Court interfered by setting aside the sentence of death and imposing a sentence of life imprisonment.

issue.issue_text: Whether new pleas can be raised in appeals under Art. 136 of the Constitution.

facts: The Court considered a precedent, *Masalti v. State of U.P.*, which was also an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
In that precedent, a point was raised before the Supreme Court that had been rejected by the trial court but was not repeated before the High Court.
The context for this consideration is often in serious criminal proceedings, such as those where a death sentence has been imposed.
law: There is no hard and fast rule that prohibits new pleas from being raised in appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution.
application: The Court reasoned that it may not be appropriate to refuse to consider relevant and material pleas of fact and law solely on the ground that they were not urged before the High Court.
This is particularly true in serious criminal cases, like those involving the death penalty.
The Court stated that in a "proper case," it is permissible for appellants to ask the Court to consider a point even if it was not raised in the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that new pleas can be raised in appeals under Article 136, as there is no strict rule prohibiting it. The Court held that, especially in serious criminal cases, it may be permissible to consider relevant pleas of fact and law even if they were not urged before the High Court.

cases.case_name: Jummen and Others v. The State of Punjab
cases.principle: No hard and fast rule can be laid down prohibiting new pleas from being raised in appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: Ram Shanker Singh & Ors. v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: Recognised the principle that no hard and fast rule can be laid down prohibiting new pleas from being raised in appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution.
A point taken before the trial court and rejected, but not repeated before the High Court, could be urged in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, no hard and fast rule prohibits the Supreme Court from considering pleas that were not properly examined or were conceded by counsel in the lower court, and it may permit an appellant to ask the Court to re-examine the entire evidence to form its own judgment.
obiter: Once the court decides to consider such pleas, it may form a view on whether a further enquiry or the taking of additional evidence is desirable before coming to its own conclusion on the entire material on record.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the conviction for murder was upheld after an independent review of the entire evidence, the sentence of death was deemed inappropriate. The Court found that special features of the case—that the murder was not premeditated, the appellant was incited by his father, and the act was not cruel or brutal—meant that the ends of justice would be met by the lesser penalty of life imprisonment.
legal_tests_applied: In proceedings for confirmation of a death sentence, an appellate court must examine the entire record to 'come to its own conclusion on the entire material on record whether conviction of the condemned prisoner is justified and the sentence of death should be confirmed.'
why_appellant_lost: The appellant lost on the issue of conviction because after the Supreme Court examined the entire evidence for itself, it was 'unable to hold that any grounds are made out for interference with the conviction.'

The prosecution witnesses were found to be credible, as they were interested in seeing the 'real murderer' of their father convicted and had no 'enmity with the appellant as could induce him to give false evidence and to substitute him as the murderer in place of the perso!1 really guilty.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded in upholding the conviction because the Supreme Court, after conducting its own review of the evidence, concluded that no grounds were made out for interference.

The Court found the testimony of the witnesses reliable, reasoning that their feelings would be 'strongest agamst. the real culprit' and they would not be expected to substitute an innocent person for the guilty one.
policy_considerations: In criminal proceedings where a death sentence is imposed, it 'may not be appropriate to refuse to consider relevant and material pl~as of fact and law only on the ground that they were not urged before the High Court.'

An appellate court does not properly discharge its duties in a death sentence confirmation case if it fails to examine the defence evidence for itself and instead relies on a concession from the appellant's counsel that there is no substance in it.

In sentencing for murder, the 'ends of justice' must be considered, and where a murder was not premeditated or particularly cruel, and where the accused was incited by another, a sentence of life imprisonment may be more appropriate than the death penalty.
